topic: V100s are not dead: a cited 80%-of-model measurement from an 8-card lawyer server
title: How Eight Used V100s Run 80% of DeepSeek v4.1 Flash at High Precision
description: Reported by Tom's Hardware: a lawyer's eight used 2018 Tesla V100s, 256 GB of memory total, run DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, estimated at 269 GB, by keeping every expert at 2-bit and promoting the 5,949 most-used to NVFP4. About 80% of decode routes land on the high-precision experts, and fidelity against Nvidia's own NVFP4 build improved. Builder's own measurements; R580 is the last driver branch for these cards.
narration_full: You buy eight used data center cards. Then DeepSeek V four point one Flash arrives, bigger than all eight. Everyone told you cards this old are scrap. One lawyer's server disagrees. Picture a lawyer who can't send case files to the cloud. His answer: eight used Tesla V one hundred cards, two hundred fifty-six gigabytes of memory in one home server. The model he wants is huge. At official precision, by his estimate, it needs two hundred sixty-nine gigabytes of model. The cards hold less than that before anything else loads. The rescue is the model's own design. It's a mixture-of-experts model, where a router wakes only a few specialists per word instead of using every parameter. So most of those gigabytes sleep most of the time. He stores every expert at two bit, the cheapest storage that works. Then the busiest get promoted to N V F P four, a sharper four-bit format, until the cards are full. Think of a workshop: every tool hangs on the wall. The few you grab all day get the good steel. His own files picked the favorites. The result: about eighty percent of its decoding, the word-by-word writing, lands on the sharpened experts. He checked it against Nvidia's own four-bit build of the same model. His box picks the same next word more often, and its answers change less. So much for scrap. The catches are honest ones. A second request at the same time shrinks the promoted set, so the solo numbers are the best case. And by his account, Nvidia's R five eighty driver branch is the last that ever supports these cards. Eight bargain-bin cards, a careful headcount, and the biggest model he owns runs at high precision all day. The model never had to fit. Only the parts in daily use had to fit well.
analogy: Workshop: every tool hangs on the wall at 2-bit, and the handful you reach for all day gets the full-quality version on the bench. Limit: which tools count as most-used was counted from his own mix of documents, and a second concurrent request shrinks the high-precision set.

notes_for_review: Spoken number budget spent on exactly the three assigned: 256 GB (s2), 269 GB with 'by his estimate' hedge (s3), 80% (s6). The 5,949 of 15,360 expert counts appear on screen only, per the assignment's required beat, without spending a spoken number. Builder identity unverified, hedged as 'a lawyer'; fidelity phrased as his own checks against Nvidia's NVFP4 build with no extra digits. One wry beat: 'So much for scrap' in s6, aimed at the cards. Workshop analogy used once with its limit clause inside s5; the concurrency shrink carries into s7 alongside the R580 end-of-support fact. No positional labels; each turn is named by what changed (cards, wall, design, promotion, result, catches). Payoff is the final spoken sentence; nothing follows it.
